Orthopedics · published research

Hand extensor tendon injury

The only direct randomized trial found no significant added benefit of low-level laser therapy for measured hand outcomes through eight weeks.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

The only direct randomized trial found no significant added benefit of low-level laser therapy for measured hand outcomes through eight weeks.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Tendons > Hand extensor tendon injuries category contains one unique human publication, a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial with 55 participants. No other direct clinical publication, animal study, or in-vitro/ex-vivo experiment was listed.

Human and clinical evidence

The trial studied repaired extensor tendon injuries in zones five through eight of the hand. Participants received usual rehabilitation with active or placebo laser treatment. The authors found no significant between-group difference in clinical outcomes at weeks four and eight (Erdoğan et al. 2025). This is direct sham-controlled evidence for the tested schedule, but one trial with short follow-up cannot determine whether a different treatment course or patient subgroup would respond differently.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal evidence was identified in this exact indication category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified for repaired hand extensor tendons.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used a 1064-nm near-infrared laser at 100 mW. Treatment was delivered with the probe held 25 mm from the skin, for 300 seconds per session and a reported energy density of 7.5 J/cm². The course comprised ten sessions over two weeks. These parameters describe one postoperative rehabilitation trial; they do not establish the effect of other wavelengths, schedules, or tendon zones.

Interpretation

The trial does not support an added clinical benefit for the tested laser schedule over sham when both groups receive rehabilitation. Evidence is absent on longer-term tendon strength and return to work or sport.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for added improvement in pain, motion, or hand function after extensor tendon repair
Publications and records1 unique title in the exact category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The exact category contains one 55-person double-blind sham-controlled randomized trial. It found no significant between-group difference in the main clinical outcomes at four or eight weeks. A single study cannot rule out smaller effects or effects under another schedule, but replication with prespecified outcomes is needed before claiming added benefit.
